title: ENDGAME
dek: What the agreement actually said, how the available strategic exits narrowed, and how the public record compares with the stories told about it.
design_contract: Human causal language comes before analyst shorthand.
Strategic complementarity is not proof of tactical tasking.
Publisher context is separate from proposition-level evidence classification.
Interviews and anecdotes are never rendered as population polling.

S01.supports: Full 14-point Islamabad MOU text; controlling public text for ¶¶1–14.

S02.supports: Senior U.S. official: sequencing is key; parties could walk away; Iran agreed toll-free Hormuz passage and talks with Oman/Gulf states.

S03.supports: Iran Supreme Leader publicly approved the MOU after assurances Iranian rights and Resistance Front interests would be protected.

S04.supports: Three commercial vessels attacked; U.S. said initial indications Iran fired; Qatar blamed Iran; Iran said vessels using routes not coordinated with it faced risk; U.S. struck IRGC/coastal systems and revoked oil license.

S05.supports: Trump declared the MOU 'over' after renewed exchanges.

S06.supports: Iran said Hormuz would remain shut until U.S. fulfilled June MOU conditions; Reuters notes U.S. called deal over July 7 and Iran later declared it suspended.

S07.supports: Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan sign Mecca Joint Defence Agreement; attack on one treated as attack on all.

S08.supports: Iran publicly says it has no reason to fear Mecca pact and welcomes regional self-reliance if inclusive.

S09.supports: Iran says it received no formal invitation to join the Mecca pact; broader regional-security discussions occurred.

S10.publisher: MM News quoting Al Mayadeen / Iranian parliament news-agency head
S10.supports: Mehdi Rahimi claimed Iran had received an invitation to join the Mecca pact; no founding-state confirmation at publication.

S11.supports: Saudi Arabia proposed 14-nation maritime-defense coalition for Red Sea/Bab el-Mandab/Gulf of Aden amid Houthi pressure.

S12.supports: Internationally recognized Yemeni government welcomed Mecca pact and linked it to terrorism, arms smuggling, attacks on neighbors and threats to maritime routes.

S13.supports: Bessent expands secondary-sanctions threat; cure period; five sectors; nearly 60 targets; major Chinese banks initially spared.

S14.supports: Iranian crude arrivals in China fell to ~534k bpd in August from ~823k in July; major state refiners remain cautious.

S15.supports: Iranian oil offers to China fell as blockade bit; Chinese refiners sought Brazilian/Iraqi alternatives.

S16.supports: UAE suspended trade/commercial/financial dealings with Iran after UAE alleged two Iranian missiles; Iran denied allegation.

S17.supports: Iran blacklists 45 tankers; threatens fines, detention/confiscation; creates petition mechanism under new Strait authority.

S18.supports: Reuters assessment of Iran escalation options; Houthi pressure on Red Sea routes complements Hormuz pressure but does not itself prove tactical Iranian tasking.

S19.supports: Trump contacted Pakistan's Asim Munir before Tehran visit, asking Pakistan to encourage Iran toward negotiations; Makkah/Houthi issues also on agenda.

S20.supports: 31,450 weighted respondents inside Iran, June 20–27; 51% disagreed missile program increased security, 47% opposed closing Hormuz, 59% opposed nuclear weapons; methodology must be shown.

S21.supports: Iranian officials worried more economic pressure could worsen hardship/unrest; July inflation 66%, food prices sharply higher; interviews with citizens.

S22.supports: Iranian families report severe household pressure, lost purchasing power and cuts to basic consumption.

S23.supports: Oil-market analysis: June MOU effectively collapsed, 60-day period expired; Hormuz flows heavily reduced.

clauses.title: Permanent ceasefire across fronts
clauses.summary: Immediate and permanent termination of military operations across the covered fronts, including Lebanon, with non-aggression and sovereignty commitments.

clauses.title: Sovereignty and non-interference
clauses.summary: Both sides commit to respect sovereignty and territorial integrity and to refrain from interference in each other’s internal affairs.

clauses.title: 60-day route to a final deal
clauses.summary: The interim bargain sets a 60-day period to negotiate a final settlement, extendable only by mutual agreement.

clauses.title: Blockade relief and later force withdrawal
clauses.summary: Washington begins removing the naval blockade immediately, completes removal within 30 days, and—if a final deal is reached—withdraws forces from Iran’s proximity on the agreed timetable.

clauses.title: Hormuz safe passage and future administration
clauses.summary: Iran owes immediate toll-free safe commercial passage for 60 days, removal of mines and obstacles, restoration of traffic, and dialogue with Oman and other Gulf littoral states on future administration and maritime services.

clauses.title: Reconstruction and economic development
clauses.summary: The United States and regional partners commit to develop a mutually agreed reconstruction and economic-development plan worth at least $300 billion, with implementation mechanics left to the final deal.

clauses.title: Sanctions-termination pathway
clauses.summary: Washington commits to terminate covered sanctions on an agreed schedule as part of a final settlement; the interim text is a pathway, not immediate permanent termination of every sanction.

clauses.title: Nuclear weapon, stockpile and enrichment
clauses.summary: Iran reaffirms it will not develop or procure nuclear weapons; enriched-stockpile disposition includes on-site downblending under IAEA supervision as a minimum, while final enrichment rules remain for the final deal.

clauses.title: Interim nuclear status quo
clauses.summary: The parties hold the nuclear position in an interim status quo while the final enrichment, inspection and implementation framework is negotiated.

clauses.title: Interim U.S. restraint and oil relief
clauses.summary: Pending a final deal, Washington undertakes not to add new sanctions or additional regional force deployments under the interim bargain and issues immediate Treasury waivers supporting Iranian crude and petroleum trade.

clauses.title: Frozen and restricted Iranian funds
clauses.summary: The agreement promises to make frozen or restricted Iranian funds fully usable through agreed release procedures; durable broad access did not mature before the bargain collapsed.

clauses.title: Executive monitoring mechanism
clauses.summary: The interim framework creates an executive-level mechanism to monitor implementation, resolve disputes and keep the sequencing process moving.

clauses.title: Sequencing and continuing implementation
clauses.summary: Progress toward final negotiations depends on continuing implementation of key interim obligations, including the ceasefire, blockade/safe-passage and economic-relief provisions.

clauses.title: Binding final-deal endorsement
clauses.summary: The contemplated final agreement is intended to receive binding United Nations Security Council endorsement rather than remain only a bilateral political understanding.

mou_death.title: MOU public; implementation begins
mou_death.detail: The interim bargain becomes the controlling public text and front-loaded implementation starts.

mou_death.title: Shipping and route disputes reappear
mou_death.detail: The maritime implementation layer becomes the practical stress point.

mou_death.title: Three tankers hit; U.S. strikes and revokes oil relief
mou_death.detail: Confirmed vessel attacks and contested attribution are followed by U.S. kinetic escalation and withdrawal of an economic concession.

mou_death.title: Washington says the MOU is over
mou_death.detail: The U.S. political position becomes explicit.

mou_death.title: Iran later declares the MOU suspended
mou_death.detail: Tehran does not treat the old instrument as normally functioning.

mou_death.title: 60-day period expires; Iran still invokes old terms
mou_death.detail: No final deal is completed, but Tehran continues using the old bargain as a negotiating baseline.

mou_status.afterlife: Iran continues citing the expired/non-controlling bargain as a baseline; citation alone does not revive its terms.

points: Washington resumed force, threats and blockade pressure.
Tehran says those acts violated the ceasefire/MOU and blocked final talks.
Iran later demanded U.S. compliance with the June terms before reopening Hormuz.
The U.S. initial assessment said Iran fired at the vessels; Iran disputed that attribution.
Qatar blamed Iran for the attack on a Qatari LNG tanker.
Iran simultaneously said vessels using routes not coordinated with Tehran faced risk.
Washington treated the sequence as a breach of ceasefire/free-navigation obligations and struck Iranian maritime and strike capability.

says: Use best efforts for safe commercial passage.
Start commercial traffic immediately and restore it as mines and military obstacles are removed.
Conduct dialogue with Oman on future administration and maritime services.
Discuss the future system with other Gulf littoral states consistent with applicable international law and coastal-state rights.
does_not_say: Iran receives exclusive sovereignty over the Strait.
Iran receives unilateral permanent transit-approval authority.
Iran receives a permanent compulsory toll on passage.
Tehran alone defines the future administration.
Oman and other littoral states are removed from future governance discussions.

tests.text: Paragraph 5 says no charge for 60 days and explicitly defers future administration and services to dialogue with Oman and others.
Paragraph 4 trades blockade removal against restored vessel traffic; paragraph 13 makes continuing implementation of key interim terms part of the route to final negotiations.

During the July 7 crisis Iran said ships using routes not coordinated with Tehran faced risk while the United States and Qatar attributed attacks to Iran. The attacks are confirmed; specific attribution remains contested by Iran.

Iran’s supreme leadership publicly approved the MOU after assurances on national rights, while a senior U.S. official publicly described sequencing and toll-free Hormuz passage before implementation. This supports knowledge of the framework, not proof of hidden intent.

paragraph5.finding: The strongest public evidence supports a maritime-implementation breakdown preceding Washington’s abandonment of the bargain. Iran’s route-control position and the July vessel-attack sequence were difficult to reconcile with paragraph 5’s safe-passage structure; Washington then escalated militarily and withdrew relief, which Tehran cited as U.S. violations. The sequence is much better supported than any claim that Iran entered the MOU with a proven secret intent to deceive.
paragraph5.confidence: HIGH on sequence; lower on subjective intent.

mou_now.text: Iran has an incentive to preserve the old MOU as a negotiating anchor because it contained concessions negotiated when Tehran’s leverage was stronger: blockade relief, oil waivers, frozen-asset access, a sanctions-termination pathway and reconstruction funding. The public record does not show that those old terms have been restored. A successor deal could reuse parts of the exchange under tighter milestones, outside verification and reversible concessions.

decisions.title: Take a tighter deal
decisions.plain: Accept that the old bargain will not simply be restored and negotiate a successor with clearer verification, Hormuz rules and staged relief.
decisions.works: It works if both sides can exchange verifiable maritime/nuclear milestones for reversible economic relief.
decisions.backfires: It fails politically if Tehran treats any tighter verification as surrender or Washington front-loads demands without credible relief.
decisions.change: Concrete successor-deal text, verified milestones, or restored relief would materially change this assessment.

decisions.title: Wait it out
decisions.plain: Absorb more economic damage and hope major counterparties refuse Washington’s secondary-sanctions pressure.
decisions.works: It works if large banks, refiners, shippers and insurers continue transacting at scale despite U.S. risk.
decisions.backfires: It backfires if counterparties quietly substitute away from Iran during the cure period.
decisions.change: Sustained or recovering trade volumes through major counterparties would weaken the current narrowing assessment.

decisions.title: Make it hurt
decisions.plain: Use Hormuz, aligned actors or renewed kinetics to raise the cost to Washington and Gulf states.
decisions.works: It can create immediate bargaining pressure if costs rise without triggering a stronger coalition response.
decisions.backfires: Regional attacks can validate the case for tighter defense integration; weak attacks can advertise dwindling capability while strong attacks risk a much more damaging response.
decisions.change: Observable coalition fragmentation rather than integration after new coercion would change the direction of this branch.

claim_vs_record.claim: Iran was invited to the Mecca pact.
claim_vs_record.record: An Iran-linked official said Iran had been invited. Iran’s Foreign Ministry later said no formal invitation had been received.

claim_vs_record.claim: China stands with Iran, so economic pressure is failing.
claim_vs_record.record: Beijing can oppose unilateral sanctions politically while commercial actors de-risk. Iranian crude arrivals fell and major state refiners remained cautious; buyers sought alternatives.

claim_vs_record.claim: Iran does not need the dollar.
claim_vs_record.record: Washington’s secondary-sanctions leverage targets banks, insurers, shippers, refiners and traders that may still value access to the U.S. or dollar-linked financial system, regardless of the invoice currency used for a particular trade.

claim_vs_record.claim: Iran survived sanctions for decades, so this changes nothing.
claim_vs_record.record: Survival is not the same as preserved trade access or bargaining capacity. Counterparty de-risking and household pressure can worsen even when the state remains intact.

claim_vs_record.claim: Every Houthi attack proves a direct Iranian order.
claim_vs_record.record: Houthi operations can complement Iranian pressure strategically without public evidence proving Tehran tactically ordered a specific attack.

international_audit: Claims that sanctions guarantee regime collapse
